origin_region: Kyoto · Uji; Aichi · Nishio; Kagoshima; Shizuoka
cultivar: Samidori, Asahi, Uji-hikari, Gokou, Okumidori, Saemidori, Yabukita
processing: Shaded for 20–30 days like gyokuro, steamed, then dried flat without any rolling in a brick tencha furnace; stems and veins are removed by cutting and air sorting, leaving thin flakes of leaf blade ready for grinding into matcha.
harvest_season: First flush in May for the drinking grades of matcha; second-flush and autumn tencha go into culinary matcha. Production has expanded sharply with matcha demand, including more machine-harvested lots.
appearance_dry: Small, papery, brittle flakes of deep green leaf with the stems and veins removed, very light for their volume.
appearance_liquor: Pale, clear green with a faint sheen.
appearance_wet: Thin, flat pieces of leaf blade, vivid green, like torn tissue paper.
taste_profile: Soft, sweet and umami-rich with a clean, almost delicate texture; far less intense than matcha made from the same leaf because you are only infusing it.

brewing.notes: Tencha is very light, so measure by weight, not spoons. Cool water, a long first steep; many people prefer it cold-brewed. It infuses gently rather than giving the punch of matcha.

vintage_note: Normally not a retail product at all: tencha is made from the spring harvest and stored cold for grinding into matcha through the year. The small amount sold as leaf is current-year first flush from matcha producers, in small bags; it is a curiosity rather than a staple and should be drunk within the year, because the thin flakes stale quickly once the bag is open.
description:
Tencha is matcha before it is ground: leaf that was shaded like gyokuro, steamed, dried flat without rolling and stripped of its stems and veins. Almost all of it goes straight into mills, so it is barely a retail tea at all, but a few matcha producers sell it as leaf and it is worth trying once, because it shows you what matcha is actually made of.

The process diverges from gyokuro right after steaming. Instead of being rolled, the leaves are blown and dried flat in a brick tencha furnace with a conveyor inside, then cut and winnowed so that only the thin leaf blade remains; the stems and veins are sold on as karigane. The result is light, brittle flakes, and the removal of everything but the blade is why matcha is so green, so smooth and so expensive. A granite stone mill turns only a few tens of grams of tencha into matcha in an hour.

As a leaf tea it is gentle. The flakes have almost no density, so measure 5 g by weight, cover with plenty of water at 60–65 °C and give it a couple of minutes; you get a pale, sweet, umami-rich cup with a clean texture and none of the intensity of matcha, because most of the leaf's goodness stays in the leaf when you only infuse it. It cold-brews beautifully. The mistake is to expect matcha in a kyusu; it is closer to a delicate gyokuro.

What little is sold comes from matcha makers in Uji, Nishio and Kagoshima, in small bags, and should be from the spring harvest; buy it from a shop that mills its own matcha. Two name traps: Chinese 'tian cha' (sweet tea) is an unrelated plant, and 'tencha' on a bulk listing does not tell you how long the leaf was shaded or which harvest it was. Production of tencha has expanded sharply with world demand for matcha, and a lot of newer tencha is second-flush, machine-harvested leaf destined for culinary grades.

Try it alongside a matcha from the same producer: same leaf, two completely different drinks.
